title: From Perception to Attention
summary: How the brain builds representations of the world and selects what matters.

lessons.title: Ventral and Dorsal Visual Streams: What vs How

levels.kid:
When you look at a cup of cocoa, your eyes send the picture to the back of your brain. From there, the picture travels down two different roads.

The **"what" road** goes down toward the sides of your head, near your ears. It figures out what the thing is: "That's my cocoa cup!"

The **"how" road** goes up toward the top of your head. It helps your hands reach out and grab the cup without spilling.

Scientists met a woman whose "what" road was hurt. She could not say which way a mail slot was tilted. But when she tried to post a letter, her hand turned the right way and slid it in! Her "how" road still worked.
levels.hs:
Vision doesn't happen in one place. Signals from the eyes reach the **primary visual cortex (V1)** at the back of the brain. From there they split into two main pathways called **visual streams**.

- The **ventral stream** runs down into the **temporal lobe**. It builds a lasting description of objects: their shape, color and identity. It's nicknamed the **"what" pathway**.
- The **dorsal stream** runs up into the **parietal lobe**. It tracks where things are and how they move, then turns that into actions like reaching and grasping. It was first called the **"where" pathway** and is now often called the **"how" pathway**.

In 1982, Leslie Ungerleider and Mortimer Mishkin showed this split in monkeys. Damage to the temporal lobe made it hard to tell objects apart. Damage to the parietal lobe made it hard to judge locations.

The best human example is a patient known as **DF**. **Carbon monoxide poisoning** damaged her ventral stream and left her with **visual form agnosia**: she could not recognize shapes or say which way a slot was tilted. Yet she could post a card through that same slot perfectly, rotating her hand to the correct angle. Her dorsal stream was still guiding her actions.

People with the opposite damage, in the parietal lobe, can recognize objects but reach for them clumsily. This problem is called **optic ataxia**.
levels.college:
The two-streams model organizes visual cortex into two processing hierarchies that leave V1.

**Ventral stream (occipitotemporal):** V1 → V2 → V4 → inferior temporal cortex (areas TEO and TE in monkeys; lateral occipital and fusiform cortex in humans). Receptive fields grow larger along the way. Neurons respond to increasingly complex features, from oriented edges to object parts to whole objects, and become more tolerant of changes in position, size and viewpoint.

**Dorsal stream (occipitoparietal):** V1 → V2 → V3 and **MT/V5** → posterior parietal cortex. This includes intraparietal sulcus areas **LIP** (eye movements), **AIP** (grasping) and the parietal reach region. MT neurons are tuned to the direction and speed of motion. Damage there causes **akinetopsia**, the loss of motion perception (patient LM, described by Zihl in 1983).

**From 'where' to 'how'.** Ungerleider and Mishkin (1982) used two monkey tasks. Inferotemporal lesions impaired an object discrimination task. Posterior parietal lesions impaired a landmark task, in which the monkey had to choose the food well closer to a landmark. In 1992, Goodale and Milner reinterpreted the split by its output rather than its input:
- Ventral: **vision for perception**. It uses allocentric (scene-based) coding, is slower, and is linked to memory and conscious recognition.
- Dorsal: **vision for action**. It uses egocentric (body-centered) coding, is fast, and works moment to moment, often outside awareness.

**The double dissociation.** Patient DF had visual form agnosia from lateral occipital damage. She failed to match a slot's orientation by turning a card, yet she posted the card accurately and scaled her grip to object width. Patients with **optic ataxia** after superior parietal damage show the reverse pattern: intact recognition but misdirected reaches, especially toward peripheral targets. When different lesions produce opposite deficits, that is strong evidence the two functions rely on separable circuits.

**Inputs.** Magnocellular signals (fast, motion-sensitive) feed the dorsal stream more heavily. Parvocellular signals (color, fine detail) feed the ventral stream more heavily. Still, these inputs mix extensively by V1 and V2.
levels.phd:
The Goodale-Milner framework predicts that the dorsal stream computes the metrics needed for action in real time and keeps no durable store. Tests of this prediction have been influential.

**Delay effects.** When DF had to wait about 2 seconds after an object disappeared before grasping it, her grip scaling collapsed. This suggests delayed actions must draw on a perceptual (ventral) representation, which she lacked. Conversely, optic ataxia patients studied by Milner and colleagues (around 2001) reached more accurately after a delay than immediately. That fits a switch to an intact ventral representation.

**Illusions and grasping.** Aglioti, DeSouza and Goodale (1995) reported that the Ebbinghaus (Titchener circles) illusion fooled perceived size but had much less effect on grip aperture. Franz and others countered that the perceptual and grasping tasks differed in attention, in how responses were calibrated, and in whether one disc or two were compared. When the tasks were matched, illusion effects on grasping often reappeared. The illusion evidence is now considered contested. The neuropsychological dissociations remain the strongest support for the model.

**Subdivisions.** Kravitz, Saleem, Baker and Mishkin (2011) proposed that the dorsal stream splits into three pathways:
- parieto-prefrontal, for spatial working memory and eye movements;
- parieto-premotor, for visually guided reaching and grasping;
- parieto-medial temporal, for navigation via posterior cingulate and retrosplenial cortex to the hippocampus.

Rizzolatti and Matelli separately distinguished a dorso-dorsal route (superior parietal lobule, online control of reaching) from a ventro-dorsal route (inferior parietal lobule, action understanding and tool use). The ventral stream likewise has multiple recurrent loops to the amygdala, striatum and prefrontal cortex (Kravitz et al., 2013).

**Not a strict partition.** Shape-selective neurons exist in AIP and in the human intraparietal sulcus, and dorsal shape signals can contribute to object recognition (work by Freud, Behrmann and colleagues). The streams also exchange information through many cross-connections. The modern view therefore treats them as interacting systems, distinguished mainly by the purpose and coordinate frame of their computations rather than by which visual features they receive.

**A third stream.** Pitcher and Ungerleider (2021) argued for a lateral pathway running from V1 through MT to the superior temporal sulcus, specialized for dynamic social cues such as moving faces and bodies.
levels.expert:
**Clinical localization.** Dorsal stream syndromes are often missed because acuity charts and naming tests come back normal.
- **Bálint's syndrome** follows bilateral parieto-occipital damage. It combines optic ataxia, simultanagnosia (perceiving only one object at a time) and oculomotor apraxia (difficulty directing gaze voluntarily). Causes include watershed infarcts after cardiac arrest.
- **Posterior cortical atrophy** (Benson's syndrome) is usually an atypical presentation of Alzheimer's pathology. It often begins with dorsal features: misjudging distances, reaching errors, losing one's place along lines of text, or getting lost, while memory is relatively spared early on. Patients frequently see optometrists for years before diagnosis.
- **Ventral damage**, for example bilateral posterior cerebral artery strokes, causes apperceptive or associative agnosias and achromatopsia. Left-sided lesions can cause pure alexia.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** Resections in the superior parietal lobule or intraparietal sulcus risk optic ataxia or impaired grasp control even when visual fields are preserved. Awake surgery and navigated TMS mapping routinely test language and motor function, but visuomotor tasks are mapped less often, and protocols are still being developed. Lesion-symptom mapping in tumor patients suggests that deficits depend on connecting white matter, such as the superior longitudinal fasciculus, as much as on cortex.

**Development: dorsal stream vulnerability.** Atkinson and Braddick found that global motion coherence thresholds (a dorsal measure) are disproportionately impaired relative to global form thresholds in Williams syndrome, in many children born very preterm, and in subsets of children with autism and dyslexia. It is still debated whether this reflects a fragile magnocellular-dorsal system or nonspecific effects on long-range networks.

**Computational models.** Deep convolutional networks trained on object recognition predict ventral stream responses well but are weaker models of dorsal areas. Networks trained on self-motion tasks fit dorsal responses better (Mineault and colleagues, 2021), a computational echo of the what-versus-how split.

**Open questions.** How do the streams coordinate so that what you recognize shapes how you act, as when you grasp a knife by its handle? DF could scale her grasp to objects but often failed to pick tools up by their functionally appropriate part. This implies that ventral knowledge selects the grasp while dorsal circuits execute it. Where that integration happens, perhaps in inferior parietal and premotor cortex, remains unresolved.

keyPoints: Visual signals leave V1 in two main streams: ventral (temporal) and dorsal (parietal)
Ventral stream = 'what': object shape, color and identity for perception and memory
Dorsal stream = 'where/how': location, motion (MT/V5) and visually guided action
Patient DF (form agnosia) and optic ataxia patients form a classic double dissociation
Dorsal coding is fast and body-centered; ventral coding is slower and scene-based
The streams interact heavily and have subdivisions; illusion-grasping evidence is contested

test.q: The ventral visual stream carries information from V1 toward the:
choices: Primary motor cortex
Cerebellar cortex
Inferior temporal cortex
Posterior parietal cortex
test.explain: The ventral stream runs V1 → V2 → V4 → inferior temporal cortex. The posterior parietal cortex is the target of the dorsal stream.

test.q: Goodale and Milner reframed the dorsal stream as a pathway mainly for:
choices: Guiding skilled actions
Recognizing familiar faces
Storing color memories
Processing word meanings
test.explain: They described the dorsal stream as 'vision for action', guiding reaching and grasping. Face recognition belongs to the ventral stream.

test.q: Patient DF, who had visual form agnosia, could still:
choices: Match a slot's tilt by eye
Post a card into a slot
Describe an object's outline
Name a shape shown to her
test.explain: DF's intact dorsal stream let her rotate a card correctly to post it, even though she could not perceive or report the slot's orientation.

test.q: Optic ataxia, misreaching despite intact recognition, follows damage to the:
choices: Superior parietal cortex
Orbitofrontal cortex
Primary auditory cortex
Inferior temporal cortex
test.explain: Optic ataxia comes from superior parietal (dorsal stream) damage. Inferior temporal damage affects recognition, not reaching.

test.q: Ungerleider and Mishkin's original 1982 labels for the two streams were:
choices: Fast versus slow
Color versus motion
Near versus far
What versus where
test.explain: They called the ventral stream 'what' and the dorsal stream 'where'. Goodale and Milner later relabeled the dorsal stream as 'how'.

test.q: Neurons in area MT/V5 are mainly tuned to:
choices: Face identity
Word reading
Visual motion
Color constancy
test.explain: MT/V5 neurons encode the direction and speed of motion and feed the dorsal stream.

test.q: Why do DF and optic ataxia patients together form a double dissociation?
choices: Both lost vision in the same half of space
Each was injured in the same brain region
Both recovered fully within a few months
Each shows the opposite spared and lost skills
test.explain: DF has impaired perception with spared action; optic ataxia patients have spared perception with impaired action. Opposite deficits from different lesions imply separable circuits.

test.q: Which description best fits dorsal stream processing?
choices: Slow, scene-based and tied to memory
Sound-based and linked to language areas
Color-based and specialized for naming
Fast, body-centered and moment to moment
test.explain: The dorsal stream codes in egocentric (body-centered) frames in real time. Slow, scene-based, memory-linked coding describes the ventral stream.

test.q: In Ungerleider and Mishkin's work, monkeys with posterior parietal lesions struggled with:
choices: Picking the food well nearer a landmark
Learning which color predicted food
Recognizing faces of familiar monkeys
Telling two objects apart by shape
test.explain: Parietal lesions impaired the landmark (spatial) task. Inferotemporal lesions impaired object discrimination.

test.q: The ventral stream is nicknamed the ___ pathway.
test.explain: The ventral stream builds object identity, so it is called the 'what' pathway.

test.q: What is the name for the loss of motion perception after MT/V5 damage?
test.explain: Akinetopsia, as in patient LM described by Zihl, shows MT's role in motion perception.

test.q: After carbon monoxide poisoning, patient DF developed visual form ___.
test.explain: Visual form agnosia is the inability to recognize shapes despite adequate basic vision.

kidTest.q: Where does the 'what' road in your brain go?
choices: Toward the front, behind your eyes
Toward the sides, near your ears
Toward the top of your head
kidTest.explain: The 'what' road goes down toward the sides of your head, near your ears.

kidTest.q: What does the 'how' road help you do?
choices: Reach and grab a cup
Remember a friend's name
Smell your hot cocoa
kidTest.explain: The 'how' road helps your hands reach and grab things.

kidTest.q: Where do your eyes send the picture first?
choices: The front of your brain
The top of your head
The back of your brain
kidTest.explain: The picture goes to the back of the brain first, then splits into two roads.

kidTest.q: The woman with a hurt 'what' road could still:
choices: Slide a letter into the slot
Say which way the slot tilted
Tell what shape the slot was
kidTest.explain: Her 'how' road still worked, so her hand turned the right way to post the letter.

kidTest.q: The 'how' road helps your h _ _ _ _ grab things.
kidTest.explain: The 'how' road guides your hands when you reach and grab.

advancedTest.q: DF's grip scaling collapsed when she had to wait about 2 seconds before grasping. What does this most strongly suggest?
choices: Her damaged ventral stream recovered and then interfered
Dorsal action metrics are computed online, not stored
Her motor cortex became fatigued during the waiting period
Grip scaling relies mainly on auditory and tactile feedback
advancedTest.explain: The dorsal stream works in real time without a durable store, so delayed actions need a ventral perceptual representation, which DF lacked.

advancedTest.q: An optic ataxia patient reaches more accurately after a delay than immediately. The best interpretation is that:
choices: Delayed reaches can draw on intact ventral perception
Peripheral targets drift into central vision during the delay
Delays lower the visual acuity needed for accurate reaching
The damaged parietal cortex recovers within a few seconds
advancedTest.explain: With the dorsal stream damaged, delayed actions can use the intact ventral (perceptual) representation. This mirrors DF's opposite pattern.

advancedTest.q: Why is the Ebbinghaus-illusion grasping evidence for two streams considered contested?
choices: Unmatched task demands could explain the difference
The illusion barely changed the perceived disc size
Grip aperture was larger than perceived disc size
Testing was limited to patients with parietal damage
advancedTest.explain: Franz and others showed that the perceptual and grasping tasks differed in attention, calibration and comparison demands. When the tasks were matched, illusion effects on grasping often reappeared.

advancedTest.q: Shape-selective neurons in AIP and the human intraparietal sulcus are most consistent with which view?
choices: The dorsal stream is a duplicate copy of the ventral stream
Object recognition happens mainly in posterior parietal cortex
Grasping is guided by color rather than by object shape
Streams differ by computational purpose, not input features
advancedTest.explain: Both streams receive shape information. They differ mainly in what they compute it for (action versus perception) and in their coordinate frames.

lessons.title: Object and Face Recognition in Temporal Cortex

levels.kid:
When you see your friend's face, your brain knows who it is in a blink. How does it do that?

Picture a team of detectives along the side of your brain, near your ears. The first detectives spot simple things, like lines and edges. They pass their clues forward. The next detectives find shapes, like circles and corners. At the end of the line, special detectives shout, "That's a cup!" or "That's Grandma!"

Some brain spots care most about faces. Others like places, bodies, or written words.

A few people have trouble with the face spot. They can see eyes and a nose just fine, but they can't tell whose face it is. This is called **face blindness**. They often know their friends by their voice or the way they walk instead.
levels.hs:
Recognizing objects happens mainly in the **ventral visual stream**. This pathway runs from the primary visual cortex at the back of the brain forward into the **inferior temporal (IT) cortex**, on the underside of the temporal lobe.

Along the way, neurons respond to more and more complex things:
- Early areas (V1, V2) detect edges and line orientations.
- V4 responds to curves and simple shapes.
- IT neurons respond to whole objects or object parts. They keep responding even when the object moves, shrinks or turns. This is called **invariance**.

In the early 1970s, Charles Gross found IT neurons in monkeys that fired best to the shape of a hand. Later, brain scans in people revealed specialized regions:
- **Fusiform face area (FFA)**: faces (Nancy Kanwisher, 1997)
- **Parahippocampal place area (PPA)**: scenes and places
- **Extrastriate body area (EBA)**: bodies
- **Visual word form area (VWFA)**: written words, a region that becomes tuned as we learn to read

Damage to face regions, often in the right fusiform gyrus after a stroke, can cause **prosopagnosia** (face blindness). About 2% of people have a developmental form present from birth.

A famous clue that faces are special: upside-down faces are much harder to recognize than upside-down houses. This is the **face inversion effect**.
levels.college:
Object recognition is hard because one object casts endless different images on the retina as position, size, lighting and viewpoint change. The ventral stream solves this by building representations that are both **selective** (cat vs dog) and **tolerant** (still a cat when it moves).

**The hierarchy.** In macaques: V1 → V2 → V4 → posterior IT (TEO) → anterior IT (TE). Along the way:
- Receptive fields grow, from under a degree near the fovea in V1 to many degrees in IT, often crossing the midline.
- Preferred features grow more complex: edges, then curvature and shape fragments in V4, then moderately complex feature combinations in TE.
- IT responds roughly 100 ms after an image appears, fast enough that core recognition is largely a feedforward sweep.

Keiji Tanaka simplified images step by step and showed that TE neurons prefer moderately complex features, with similar preferences clustered in columns.

**Face patches.** Doris Tsao, Winrich Freiwald and Margaret Livingstone used fMRI in macaques to find cortical patches responding more to faces, then recorded inside them. In the middle face patch, about 97% of visually responsive neurons were face selective (Tsao et al., 2006). Macaques have about six connected patches per hemisphere.

**Human category-selective regions** on the ventral surface include the FFA and occipital face area (faces), PPA (scenes), EBA (bodies) and VWFA (words, usually left hemisphere). Face and word regions sit laterally on the fusiform gyrus; place regions sit medially.

**Holistic face processing.** Faces are processed as integrated wholes:
- Inversion effect (Yin, 1969)
- Composite face effect: identical top halves look different when aligned with different bottom halves
- Part-whole effect: a nose is recognized better inside a whole face than alone

**Lesion evidence.** Acquired prosopagnosia usually follows right or bilateral occipitotemporal damage, such as posterior cerebral artery stroke, and can spare object recognition. Some patients show the reverse, giving a rough double dissociation.
levels.phd:
**Population codes and untangling.** DiCarlo and Cox proposed that the ventral stream progressively untangles object manifolds so that identity becomes linearly decodable. Hung et al. (2005) showed that a linear classifier reading a few hundred IT sites could categorize objects within about 100 ms of onset, generalizing across position and size. Haxby et al. (2001) showed with multivoxel fMRI patterns that categories could still be decoded from ventral temporal cortex after excluding the maximally responsive voxels, fueling the debate between modular and distributed accounts.

**The face code.** Representations transform along the macaque face network: ML/MF neurons are view-specific, AL shows mirror-symmetric view tuning, and AM is largely view-invariant for identity (Freiwald & Tsao, 2010). Chang & Tsao (2017) described faces in a 50-dimensional shape-appearance space and found that face cells act as linear projections onto preferred axes: firing ramps along one axis and barely changes for variation orthogonal to it. Responses of about 200 cells allowed reconstruction of novel faces. This argues against exemplar-tuned grandmother cells in IT itself.

**Causality.** Afraz, Kiani & Esteky (2006) microstimulated face-selective IT sites and biased monkeys toward reporting noisy images as faces. In humans, Parvizi et al. (2012) stimulated the FFA through implanted electrodes; the patient reported faces morphing ("you just turned into somebody else") while objects looked normal.

**Domain specificity vs expertise.** Kanwisher argues for domain-specific face machinery; Gauthier's expertise hypothesis holds that the FFA serves fine-grained discrimination in any well-practiced category (car experts, trained 'Greeble' novices). Evidence is mixed, and well-controlled studies find face selectivity larger than expertise effects.

**Development.** Arcaro, Livingstone and colleagues (2017) raised macaques without seeing faces. They lacked face patches yet developed other category domains, and looked preferentially at hands. This supports an innate retinotopic proto-organization sculpted by experience rather than a fully prespecified face module.

**Deep networks.** Yamins, DiCarlo and colleagues (2014) found that performance-optimized convolutional neural networks predicted IT responses better than earlier models, with deeper layers mapping onto IT.
levels.expert:
**Neurosurgical relevance.** The ventral temporal surface is a common target in epilepsy and tumor surgery, and face-selective cortex in the mid-fusiform gyrus lies near posterior cerebral artery territory. Intracranial work shows hemispheric asymmetry: right fusiform stimulation more readily distorts perceived faces, while left-sided stimulation more often produces non-face effects (Rangarajan et al., 2014). Left ventral temporal resections that encroach on the VWFA can cause pure alexia; right anterior temporal resections can impair recognition of familiar people. Because FFA and VWFA locations vary between individuals, group atlases are unreliable, and individual fMRI localizers plus stimulation mapping are preferred.

**Person identity beyond IT.** Familiar-face recognition extends into anterior temporal and medial temporal structures. Quiroga et al. (2005) recorded hippocampal and entorhinal neurons in epilepsy patients that fired to one person across photos, drawings and the written name: **concept cells**, quite unlike axis-coded IT face cells. Capgras delusion, the belief that a loved one is an impostor, is explained by Ellis and Young as a disconnection between face recognition and affective familiarity; patients may lack skin conductance responses to familiar faces. Clinical assessment uses the Cambridge Face Memory Test and Benton test, with super-recognizers at the high extreme.

**Recent advances.**
- Bao, She, McGill & Tsao (2020) proposed an object space map: IT is organized along animate-inanimate and stubby-spiky axes, with face patches as one region of it.
- Bashivan, Kar & DiCarlo (2019) and Ponce et al. (2019) used deep networks to synthesize images that drive V4 or IT neurons beyond their responses to natural images.
- Ratan Murty et al. (2020) found FFA responses to touched faces in congenitally blind people, complicating purely visual-experience accounts.
- Kar et al. (2019) showed that images hard for feedforward networks are solved later in IT responses, implicating recurrence.

**Pitfalls and open questions.** CNNs lean on texture more than shape (Geirhos et al., 2019) and fall for adversarial perturbations, so high neural predictivity does not prove a shared mechanism. fMRI selectivity depends on the contrast and threshold chosen. How feedback and recurrence contribute under clutter and occlusion remains unresolved.

keyPoints: Object recognition flows along the ventral stream from V1 to inferior temporal (IT) cortex
IT neurons are selective for objects yet tolerant to changes in size, position and view (invariance)
Humans have category regions: FFA for faces, PPA for places, EBA for bodies, VWFA for words
Macaque face patches contain mostly face-selective cells that code faces along axes of face space
Faces are processed holistically, shown by the inversion and composite effects
Right fusiform damage can cause prosopagnosia; stimulating the FFA distorts perceived faces

test.q: Which region at the end of the ventral visual stream is central to object recognition?
choices: Primary motor cortex
Inferior temporal cortex
Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex
Posterior parietal cortex
test.explain: The ventral stream ends in inferior temporal (IT) cortex, where neurons respond to whole objects. Posterior parietal cortex belongs to the dorsal stream.

test.q: An IT neuron keeps firing to a cat whether the cat is small, large or shifted to one side. This property is called:
choices: Invariance
Lateral inhibition
Adaptation
Retinotopy
test.explain: Invariance (tolerance) means the response holds across changes in size, position or viewpoint. Retinotopy describes maps tied to locations on the retina, which is the opposite idea.

test.q: Who reported the fusiform face area in humans in 1997?
choices: Keiji Tanaka
Charles Gross
David Hubel
Nancy Kanwisher
test.explain: Nancy Kanwisher and colleagues described the FFA with fMRI in 1997. Gross found hand-selective cells in monkeys, and Tanaka studied feature columns in TE.

test.q: The PPA responds most strongly to which kind of image?
choices: Words
Faces
Places
Bodies
test.explain: The parahippocampal place area prefers scenes and places. Faces drive the FFA, bodies the EBA, and words the VWFA.

test.q: Upside-down faces are much harder to recognize than upside-down houses. This suggests faces are processed:
choices: By color more than shape
As one integrated whole
Mainly by the dorsal stream
As separate isolated parts
test.explain: The inversion effect shows that faces depend on holistic processing, which flipping disrupts. Objects processed by their parts suffer much less.

test.q: Acquired prosopagnosia most often follows damage to the:
choices: Cerebellar vermis
Primary visual cortex
Left frontal lobe
Right fusiform gyrus
test.explain: Face blindness after stroke usually involves right or bilateral occipitotemporal cortex, including the fusiform gyrus. Damage to primary visual cortex causes loss of vision rather than a selective face problem.

test.q: In Tsao and colleagues' 2006 study, about what share of visually responsive neurons in a macaque face patch were face selective?
choices: About 25%
About 50%
About 75%
About 97%
test.explain: Recording inside the fMRI-defined middle face patch found about 97% of visually responsive cells were face selective, which is strong evidence for a dedicated face module.

test.q: Compared with V1, receptive fields in IT cortex are usually:
choices: Small and tuned to fast motion
Similar in size but tuned to color
Small and tuned to simple edges
Large and tuned to complex shapes
test.explain: Moving up the hierarchy, receptive fields grow and preferred features become more complex. Small, edge-tuned fields describe V1 itself.

test.q: The visual word form area becomes tuned mainly because people:
choices: Learn to speak
Recognize faces
Track motion
Learn to read
test.explain: The VWFA becomes selective for written words through reading experience. Speaking is auditory and motor, so it does not shape this visual region.

test.q: What is the medical term for face blindness?
test.explain: Prosopagnosia comes from Greek prosopon (face) and agnosia (not knowing). It can be acquired or developmental.

test.q: In the ___ face effect, identical top halves of faces look different when aligned with different bottom halves.
test.explain: The composite face effect shows that the parts of a face fuse into a whole. Misaligning the halves removes the illusion.

test.q: Charles Gross found IT neurons in monkeys that fired best to the shape of a ___.
test.explain: Gross's early 1970s 'hand cells' were among the first evidence that IT neurons respond to complex objects.

kidTest.q: Where are the brain 'detectives' that recognize things?
choices: In the back of the neck
Along the side, near the ears
At the very front, above the eyes
kidTest.explain: Object and face detectives sit along the side and bottom of the brain, near your ears.

kidTest.q: What do the first detectives in the line spot?
choices: Whole faces
Lines and edges
Names of people
kidTest.explain: The first detectives find simple lines and edges. Later detectives put the clues together into whole things.

kidTest.q: What is face blindness?
choices: Not seeing colors like red or green
Not knowing whose face it is
Not seeing well when it is dark
kidTest.explain: People with face blindness see the eyes and nose fine, but they have trouble telling who the face belongs to.

kidTest.q: How might a face-blind person know a friend?
choices: By the shape of the nose
By the color of their eyes
By their voice or walk
kidTest.explain: Voice and walk don't depend on the face spot, so they are good clues.

kidTest.q: Some brain spots care most about f _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Special brain spots work hardest when you look at faces.

advancedTest.q: A face cell's firing rises linearly as faces vary along one direction in face space and barely changes along orthogonal directions. Which conclusion follows?
choices: Each cell stores one specific familiar individual's face
Identity is coded jointly across many ramp-tuned cells
Identity is decoded from precise single-spike timing
Cells respond to low-level contrast rather than to shape
advancedTest.explain: Linear projection onto one axis means a single cell cannot identify a face. Identity emerges from the combined pattern, which is how about 200 cells could reconstruct novel faces. This argues against grandmother cells in IT.

advancedTest.q: Categories could still be decoded from ventral temporal cortex after the most category-selective voxels were removed. This finding is most often cited to support:
choices: Dorsal-stream control of object identity
Retinotopic coding of each category
Distributed, overlapping category codes
Strict modules sharing no information
advancedTest.explain: Haxby's result shows that category information is spread across weakly responsive cortex too. That challenges a purely modular view, though it does not rule out specialized regions.

advancedTest.q: Macaques raised without seeing faces lacked face patches but developed other category domains. Which interpretation best fits?
choices: Face recognition is taken over by the dorsal stream in these animals
Face patches require language learning before they can emerge
Experience shapes an innate scaffold into face domains
Face patches are genetically fixed and appear regardless of input
advancedTest.explain: Other domains still formed on a pre-existing organization, but face patches needed face experience. This points to experience sculpting an innate scaffold. Language is irrelevant in monkeys, and no dorsal takeover was described.

advancedTest.q: Why is electrical stimulation of the human fusiform face area considered stronger evidence than fMRI for its role in face perception?
choices: It measures blood flow with finer spatial detail
It removes the need for any behavioral face task
It shows a causal effect on what faces look like
It records from far more neurons at the same time
advancedTest.explain: fMRI shows correlation. Stimulation that makes faces morph while objects look normal shows that activity in this region causally shapes face perception. Stimulation does not measure blood flow.

lessons.title: Feature Binding and Bottom-Up Salience

levels.kid:
When you look at a red ball, your brain does not see it all at once. One team of brain cells notices the color red. Another team notices the round shape. Another team notices if it is moving. Then your brain has to glue these pieces back together into one ball. Scientists call this **binding**. Paying attention works like the glue.

Some things grab your eyes all by themselves. Picture one red apple in a big pile of green apples. It jumps out right away, because it looks different from everything around it. Scientists say it is **salient** (SAY-lee-ent).

Your brain keeps a kind of map of what stands out. It looks at the most salient spot first. Then it moves on to a new spot, so it does not keep checking the same place over and over.
levels.hs:
Your visual system splits a scene into separate **features**. Different groups of neurons respond to color, orientation (the tilt of edges), motion and depth. This creates a puzzle called the **binding problem**: if red and round are coded by different neurons, how does the brain know they belong to the same object, the apple, and not to the banana beside it?

Psychologist Anne Treisman proposed **Feature Integration Theory** (1980). Her key evidence came from **visual search** tasks:
- **Feature search**: find a red letter among green letters. The target seems to **pop out**, and search time barely changes whether there are 5 or 50 distractors.
- **Conjunction search**: find a red X among green Xs and red Os. Now you must combine two features, and search time grows with each added item.

Treisman argued that single features are detected in parallel, but combining them needs **focused attention**, applied to one location at a time. When attention is overloaded, people make **illusory conjunctions**: after a brief flash of a red X and a green O, they may report a red O.

The pop-out effect shows **bottom-up salience**: some items grab attention because they differ from their surroundings, not because you were looking for them. A flashing ambulance light in traffic is a real example. By contrast, **top-down** attention is guided by your goals, like searching for a friend's yellow jacket.
levels.college:
**Feature Integration Theory (FIT).** Treisman and Gelade (1980) proposed two stages. A preattentive stage builds separate **feature maps** (color, orientation, size, motion) in parallel across the visual field. An attentive stage binds features at one location using a **master map of locations**: focused spatial attention acts as the glue.

Behavioral signatures:
- **Search slopes**: feature search is nearly flat (a few ms per item); conjunction search is steep, often 20-30 ms per item when the target is present and roughly double when it is absent, consistent with a serial, self-terminating scan.
- **Illusory conjunctions** rise when attention is diverted or displays are brief.
- **Balint's syndrome**: after bilateral parietal damage, patient RM could perceive only one object at a time (simultanagnosia) and made many illusory conjunctions even with long viewing, linking parietal spatial attention to binding.

Wolfe's **Guided Search** model refined FIT: preattentive feature information guides attention toward likely targets, so conjunction search is often more efficient than a pure serial scan.

**Bottom-up salience.** Koch and Ullman (1985) proposed a **saliency map**, a topographic map encoding how conspicuous each location is. Itti, Koch and Niebur (1998) implemented it:
- Filter the image into intensity, color-opponent and orientation channels at several scales.
- Compute **center-surround** differences: a location is salient if it contrasts with its surroundings.
- Normalize and sum the maps; a **winner-take-all** process selects the peak.
- **Inhibition of return** suppresses the attended location so attention shifts to new places.

Neural candidates for salience and priority maps include area **LIP** in posterior parietal cortex, the **frontal eye fields (FEF)**, the **superior colliculus** and V1.

**Capture debate.** Theeuwes found that a salient color singleton slows search even when irrelevant, supporting automatic bottom-up capture. Folk, Remington and Johnston (1992) showed **contingent capture**: singletons capture attention mainly when they match the observer's current search goal (attentional set).
levels.phd:
**Candidate binding mechanisms.** Three broad solutions compete. (1) **Conjunctive coding**: dedicated neurons tuned to feature combinations. This works for common conjunctions but faces combinatorial explosion for arbitrary novel ones. (2) **Binding by synchrony**: Gray and Singer (1989) recorded stimulus-dependent gamma-band oscillations (roughly 40 Hz) in cat visual cortex, with spatially separated columns synchronizing when driven by a single coherent bar but not by two separate bars. Von der Malsburg's temporal correlation hypothesis held that synchronous firing tags features of one object. Shadlen and Movshon (1999) mounted the classic critique: correlated firing may arise from shared input or recurrent dynamics, there is no demonstrated downstream mechanism that reads synchrony as a binding code, and the hypothesis says how binding is signaled, not how the correct grouping is computed. (3) **Attention-based binding**, as in FIT, where parietal spatial selection gates which features are integrated.

Wolfe's analysis of thousands of search experiments found slopes form a continuum rather than a feature/conjunction dichotomy, undermining a strict serial/parallel split. Guided Search 6.0 now emphasizes a **priority map** that combines bottom-up salience, top-down guidance, scene structure and history.

**Where is salience computed?** Zhaoping Li's **V1 saliency hypothesis** proposes that V1 itself creates a bottom-up saliency map via iso-feature suppression through intracortical horizontal connections; the most active V1 neuron at a location sets its salience. A striking test: an **ocular singleton**, an item shown to one eye only and perceptually indistinguishable from the rest, still captures attention (Zhaoping 2008). Eye-of-origin signals are abundant in V1 but scarce in higher areas, so this favors an early locus.

In monkeys, Gottlieb, Kusunoki and Goldberg (1998) showed that LIP neurons responded weakly when a stable stimulus entered the receptive field via a saccade but strongly to an abrupt onset or a task-relevant stimulus, implying LIP encodes attentional priority rather than mere visual presence. White and colleagues (2017) found that superficial superior colliculus neurons track bottom-up saliency during free viewing of natural video.

Awh, Belopolsky and Theeuwes (2012) argued the bottom-up/top-down dichotomy is incomplete: **selection history**, including prior reward and repetition, biases priority independently of current goals or physical salience.
levels.expert:
**Clinical translation.** Binding and salience failures are visible at the bedside. Balint's syndrome (simultanagnosia, optic ataxia, oculomotor apraxia) follows bilateral parieto-occipital injury, classically watershed infarcts after hypotension, and is a hallmark of **posterior cortical atrophy**, usually an Alzheimer variant. Patients may read single words yet fail to describe a complex picture. In unilateral neglect, contralesional stimuli are often detected when presented alone but missed when a competing ipsilesional stimulus appears (**extinction**); raising contralesional salience, such as abrupt onsets or high contrast, can partially restore detection, a principle used in rehabilitation.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** During awake right parietal resections, Thiebaut de Schotten and colleagues (2005) showed that stimulating white matter near the superior longitudinal fasciculus caused rightward deviation on line bisection, evidence that disconnection of fronto-parietal pathways, not just cortex, produces spatial attention deficits. Intraoperative line bisection is now used to map these tracts.

**A terminology trap.** Perceptual salience (stimulus contrast) differs from **motivational or incentive salience** (Berridge), which is tied to mesolimbic dopamine. Kapur's (2003) **aberrant salience** model of psychosis proposes that dysregulated dopamine assigns significance to neutral stimuli, and that D2 antagonist antipsychotics dampen this attribution. Do not conflate this with Itti-Koch salience; the neural substrates and pharmacology differ.

**Methodological pitfalls.**
- Search slopes do not uniquely diagnose serial processing; capacity-limited parallel models can mimic them (Townsend's mimicry problem).
- Saliency models must be scored against fixation data with corrections for **center bias**, since a central Gaussian alone predicts many fixations.
- Deep models such as DeepGaze II approach benchmark ceilings, but Henderson and Hayes (2017) found **meaning maps**, built from human ratings of local semantic content, predict scene fixations better than image salience, suggesting pure bottom-up salience matters less in real scenes than in lab displays.

**Open questions.** Is there a single master saliency map, or distributed priority signals across V1, superior colliculus, pulvinar, LIP and FEF? How do recurrent feedback signals, which Lamme links to perceptual grouping, interact with attention in binding? And how should causal tools such as optogenetics in primates or intracranial recordings in epilepsy patients adjudicate the synchrony debate?

keyPoints: The binding problem: separately coded features must be combined into single objects
Feature Integration Theory: features are registered in parallel, attention binds them
Feature search pops out with flat slopes; conjunction search slows as items are added
Illusory conjunctions and Balint's syndrome link parietal attention to binding
Saliency maps rank locations by local contrast; inhibition of return moves attention on
Priority maps in LIP, FEF, superior colliculus and possibly V1 combine salience, goals and history

test.q: What is the binding problem in perception?
choices: Combining separate features into one object
Joining sensory signals to matching motor commands
Merging the two eyes' images into one depth view
Linking a word's sound to its stored meaning
test.explain: Color, shape and motion are coded by different neurons, so the brain must work out which features belong together. Depth from two eyes is a different process called stereopsis.

test.q: In visual search, how does the time to find a red target among green distractors change as the number of distractors increases?
choices: Rises steeply with each added distractor
Doubles whenever the display color changes
Falls as more distractors are added
Stays nearly flat as the set grows
test.explain: A single-feature target pops out, so search slopes are nearly flat. Steep slopes are typical of conjunction search.

test.q: According to Feature Integration Theory, what binds color and shape in a conjunction search?
choices: Focused spatial attention
Motor planning in premotor cortex
Retinal ganglion cell filtering
Preattentive parallel processing
test.explain: Treisman proposed that attention to one location at a time glues features together. Preattentive processing registers features in parallel but does not bind them.

test.q: A person briefly sees a red X and a green O. Which report is an illusory conjunction?
choices: Reporting a red O and a green X
Seeing the letters drift across the screen
Reporting three letters instead of two
Not noticing that any letters appeared
test.explain: An illusory conjunction recombines real features wrongly, here swapping the colors between letters. It shows features can be detected without being correctly bound.

test.q: Balint's syndrome, in which patients struggle to bind features and see more than one object at a time, follows damage to:
choices: Right cerebellar hemisphere
Bilateral parietal cortex
Left inferior temporal cortex
Bilateral occipital poles
test.explain: Patient RM had bilateral parietal damage and made many illusory conjunctions, linking parietal spatial attention to binding.

test.q: In the Itti-Koch saliency model, how is a location's conspicuousness computed?
choices: By counting the objects in the whole scene
By matching it to stored object templates
By contrasting it with its surroundings
By ranking objects by their reward value
test.explain: The model uses center-surround differences in intensity, color and orientation. Template matching describes object recognition, not bottom-up salience.

test.q: Why does a saliency-map model need inhibition of return?
choices: So attention shifts to new places
So eye movements are canceled during blinks
So the brightest item stays attended longer
So features are bound before being detected
test.explain: Without suppressing the winning location, winner-take-all would keep selecting the same peak. Inhibition of return lets attention move on.

test.q: Which region contains a priority map whose neurons fire strongly to abruptly appearing stimuli?
choices: Primary motor cortex
Area LIP
Hippocampal area CA1
Fusiform face area
test.explain: The lateral intraparietal area responds strongly to abrupt onsets and task-relevant stimuli, signaling attentional priority. The fusiform face area is specialized for face recognition.

test.q: Contingent capture experiments (Folk and colleagues) suggest a salient singleton grabs attention mainly when it:
choices: Appears right at the center of gaze
Fits the observer's current search goal
Has been rewarded on many earlier trials
Is the brightest item in the whole display
test.explain: Contingent capture means a singleton captures attention mainly if it matches the attentional set. Reward history is a separate influence called selection history.

test.q: A target that differs from distractors by a single feature seems to ___ out instantly.
test.explain: The pop-out effect reflects parallel detection of a unique feature.

test.q: Which psychologist proposed Feature Integration Theory in 1980?
test.explain: Anne Treisman, with Garry Gelade, proposed that attention binds features registered in parallel.

test.q: The binding-by-synchrony hypothesis proposes that neurons coding one object fire together in the ___ frequency band.
test.explain: Gray and Singer found stimulus-dependent synchrony near 40 Hz, in the gamma band, in cat visual cortex.

kidTest.q: How does your brain first look at color and shape?
choices: With different teams of cells
With one cell for everything
With the muscles around your eyes
kidTest.explain: Different teams of brain cells notice color, shape and motion separately.

kidTest.q: Why does one red apple jump out in a pile of green apples?
choices: Its color differs from its neighbors
It is sitting farther away than the rest
It is heavier than the green ones nearby
kidTest.explain: Things that look different from what is around them grab your eyes.

kidTest.q: What helps your brain glue color and shape together?
choices: Paying attention
Closing your eyes
Looking away quickly
kidTest.explain: Attention works like glue that joins the pieces into one object.

kidTest.q: After your eyes check one spot, what does your brain do next?
choices: Goes back to it right away
Moves on to a new spot
Keeps staring at that spot
kidTest.explain: The brain moves on so it does not keep checking the same place.

kidTest.q: Something that grabs your eyes because it stands out is called s _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Salient means it stands out from everything around it.

advancedTest.q: In conjunction search, target-absent slopes are often about twice target-present slopes. The classic interpretation is that:
choices: Pop-out signals are twice as weak in displays lacking a target
Attention checks items in parallel but slows when the target is missing
Distractors are suppressed twice as strongly when no target exists
Items are checked one at a time, stopping once the target is found
advancedTest.explain: In a serial self-terminating search, observers check about half the items on average when the target is present but all items when it is absent. Note that parallel models can mimic this pattern, so it is not decisive.

advancedTest.q: Shadlen and Movshon's main objection to binding by synchrony was that:
choices: Binding is largely solved in the retina before signals reach cortex
Cortical neurons fire too slowly to carry a precise temporal code
Correlated firing may reflect shared input, not a readable code
Gamma-band oscillations are too rare in awake visual cortex to matter
advancedTest.explain: They argued synchrony could be a byproduct of shared input or network dynamics, with no shown readout mechanism, and that it does not explain how the correct grouping is computed.

advancedTest.q: LIP neurons responded weakly to a stable stimulus brought into the receptive field by a saccade but strongly to an abrupt onset. This suggests LIP mainly signals:
choices: The raw luminance of whatever happens to fall in the receptive field
The identity of objects, independent of their spatial location
Attentional priority of a location, not just its contents
The motor command for the saccade that was just being executed
advancedTest.explain: The same visual stimulus evoked different responses depending on its salience or relevance, so LIP tracks priority rather than mere visual presence.

advancedTest.q: An ocular singleton, shown to one eye only and perceptually identical to other items, can still capture attention. Why does this support the V1 saliency hypothesis?
choices: Binocular fusion happens in the retina before reaching cortex
Eye-of-origin signals are abundant in V1 but scarce in higher areas
Capture without awareness shows salience is computed in frontal cortex
Higher areas such as LIP code eye of origin more strongly than V1
advancedTest.explain: Because eye-of-origin information is largely lost beyond V1, capture by an invisible ocular singleton implies salience is computed at an early stage like V1.

lessons.title: Attention Networks: Alerting, Orienting and Executive Control

levels.kid:
Your brain has three helpers for paying attention. Imagine you are a goalkeeper in football.

- The **alert** helper wakes you up and says "Get ready!" It works like the referee's whistle.
- The **orienting** helper points your attention, like a spotlight, toward where the ball is coming from.
- The **control** helper keeps you focused. It stops you from doing the wrong thing, like diving the wrong way when a player tries to trick you.

Scientists test these helpers with a game. Arrows appear on a screen, and you press a button for the way the middle arrow points. Warning signs and tricky arrows show how well each helper is working. The helpers live in different parts of the brain, but they work together as a team.
levels.hs:
**Attention** is the brain's way of selecting some information for deeper processing while ignoring the rest. In 1990, Michael Posner and Steven Petersen proposed that attention is not one thing. They described three cooperating **networks**, each run by different brain areas.

- **Alerting** means getting ready and staying ready. A warning signal, like a yellow traffic light, speeds your reaction. This network depends on the **locus coeruleus**, a tiny brainstem nucleus that releases **norepinephrine**, along with right frontal and parietal cortex.
- **Orienting** means choosing where to look or listen. You can orient **overtly** by moving your eyes, or **covertly** by shifting attention while your eyes stay still. Parietal cortex, the frontal eye fields and the superior colliculus are key players.
- **Executive control** resolves conflict between competing responses. A classic test is the **Stroop task**, where you name the ink color of the word RED printed in blue. The **anterior cingulate cortex** and lateral prefrontal cortex lead here.

A real example is driving. Alerting keeps you ready. Orienting moves your focus to a child near the road. Executive control stops you from following the habit of speeding through a light that just turned red.

Researchers measure all three networks with the **Attention Network Test (ANT)**. You press a key for the direction of a central arrow surrounded by other arrows, sometimes after a warning cue. Different combinations of cues and arrows isolate each network.
levels.college:
Posner and Petersen's model treats attention as three anatomically and chemically distinct systems that normally work together.

**Alerting** achieves and maintains a state of readiness. **Tonic alertness** is sustained vigilance over minutes. **Phasic alertness** is a brief boost after a warning signal. The core of this network is the **locus coeruleus-norepinephrine (LC-NE)** system, which projects to right-lateralized frontal and parietal cortex and to the thalamus. A warning tone speeds reaction time, often at a small cost in accuracy.

**Orienting** selects a location or object. Two distinctions matter:
- **Overt vs covert**: orienting with or without eye movements.
- **Endogenous vs exogenous**: voluntary orienting (an arrow tells you where to look) or reflexive orienting (a sudden flash captures you).

In the **Posner cueing task**, a valid cue speeds detection and an invalid cue slows it; the difference is the **validity effect**. After an exogenous cue, the advantage reverses after roughly 300 ms into **inhibition of return**, a bias against re-inspecting the same spot.

Corbetta and Shulman (2002) split orienting into two systems:
- A bilateral **dorsal attention network** (frontal eye fields, intraparietal sulcus) for top-down orienting.
- A right-lateralized **ventral attention network** (temporoparietal junction, ventral frontal cortex) that interrupts ongoing focus when something unexpected but relevant appears.

The superior colliculus and pulvinar contribute subcortically, and **acetylcholine** from the basal forebrain modulates orienting.

**Executive control** resolves conflict among thoughts and responses. The **anterior cingulate cortex** and lateral prefrontal cortex are engaged by Stroop and flanker conflict, with strong **dopamine** modulation.

The **ANT** (Fan et al., 2002) combines cueing with a flanker task. Each network is scored by subtracting reaction times (RT):
- Alerting = no-cue RT minus double-cue RT
- Orienting = center-cue RT minus spatial-cue RT
- Conflict = incongruent RT minus congruent RT

In the original healthy sample, the alerting and orienting effects were each roughly 50 ms and conflict roughly 85 ms. The three scores were only weakly correlated, which supported the idea of separable networks.
levels.phd:
The network model grew from lesion and chronometric work. Posner and colleagues (1984) found that patients with parietal lesions were disproportionately slowed when an invalid cue forced them to pull attention away from the ipsilesional side toward the contralesional field. This led to a **disengage-move-engage** account:
- Disengage was linked to parietal cortex.
- Move was linked to the superior colliculus; covert orienting is slowed in the vertical direction in progressive supranuclear palsy.
- Engage was linked to the pulvinar.

Corbetta and Shulman's dual-network model reframed this. The dorsal network (FEF, IPS/SPL) holds spatial priority maps and biases sensory cortex. The right-lateralized ventral network (TPJ, ventral frontal cortex) acts as a **circuit breaker** for behaviorally relevant, unexpected stimuli. Corbetta and colleagues (2005) proposed that neglect often follows ventral damage that leaves dorsal regions structurally intact but functionally unbalanced between the hemispheres. This interhemispheric imbalance tracked both severity and recovery.

Much of the neuromodulator mapping came from Marrocco's monkey pharmacology. The alpha2-adrenergic agonists clonidine and guanfacine, which reduce LC-NE release, selectively reduced the alerting benefit of warning cues. Cholinergic manipulations (scopolamine, nicotine) instead altered cue validity effects.

**Adaptive gain theory** (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005) adds dynamics to the LC story:
- In a **phasic mode** (moderate tonic LC firing with strong task-locked bursts), behavior is focused and exploitative.
- In a **tonic mode** (high baseline firing, weak phasic responses), behavior becomes distractible and exploratory.

For executive control, Botvinick and colleagues' (2001) **conflict-monitoring** model proposes that dorsal ACC detects response conflict and signals lateral PFC to increase control. This explains conflict adaptation, the smaller interference seen after an incongruent trial. Dosenbach et al. (2007) split control into a **cingulo-opercular** network for stable task-set maintenance and a **frontoparietal** network for trial-by-trial adjustment. Petersen and Posner's 2012 update incorporated this division.

Independence of the networks is now viewed as partial. In the ANT-I (Callejas et al., 2004), a warning tone speeds orienting but enlarges the conflict effect, suggesting that phasic alerting transiently suppresses executive control. Early reports linking DRD4 and MAOA variants to conflict scores came from small samples, and candidate-gene findings in cognition have largely failed to replicate in large studies.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the three networks map onto distinct bedside failures.

**Orienting and neglect.** Hemispatial neglect after right-hemisphere stroke is the most dramatic orienting disorder. Patients ignore left space, bisect lines to the right of center and miss left-sided targets on cancellation tests. Neglect correlates with damage to the right inferior parietal lobule and TPJ, and critically with white matter damage. Thiebaut de Schotten et al. (2005) showed during awake surgery that stimulating the second branch of the **superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF II)** produced rightward line-bisection errors. Some neurosurgical teams therefore add line bisection to awake mapping of right parietal tumors. It is a reminder that the "non-eloquent" right hemisphere is cognitively eloquent.

**Alerting as therapy.** Low arousal worsens neglect. Robertson et al. (1998) showed that unpredictable warning tones temporarily abolished patients' spatial bias. This interaction between alerting and orienting inspired alertness training in rehabilitation.

**Delirium.** Inattention is a required feature of the Confusion Assessment Method, so delirium is fundamentally a disorder of attention networks. It is often linked to cholinergic deficits and noradrenergic dysregulation, and anticholinergic medication burden is a modifiable risk factor.

**ADHD pharmacology.** Stimulants raise prefrontal dopamine and norepinephrine. Atomoxetine blocks NE reuptake. Guanfacine, an alpha2A agonist, is thought to strengthen prefrontal network firing, based on Arnsten's work. Yet ANT profiles in ADHD are inconsistent across studies, which warns against equating a diagnosis with a single network deficit.

**Measurement pitfalls.** ANT scores are difference scores, and they inherit noise from both conditions being subtracted. Test-retest reliability is moderate for conflict but notably poorer for alerting and orienting. Low reliability caps the correlations you can observe, so null findings in small samples are weakly informative. Pupil diameter is a popular LC proxy, but Joshi et al. (2016) showed it also tracks superior colliculus and cingulate activity.

**Open questions.** Is executive control one system or several? Do the three networks reflect real causes or just convenient task categories? Critics such as Anderson (2011) argue that "attention" names a set of effects rather than a mechanism. This pushes the field toward circuit-level models of priority and gain.

keyPoints: Posner and Petersen split attention into alerting, orienting and executive control networks
Alerting relies on locus coeruleus norepinephrine and right frontoparietal cortex
Orienting can be covert or overt, and endogenous or exogenous; acetylcholine modulates it
Dorsal network (FEF, IPS) directs focus; right ventral network (TPJ) reorients to surprises
Executive control resolves conflict via anterior cingulate and lateral prefrontal cortex, with dopamine
The Attention Network Test scores each network by reaction-time subtractions; the networks interact

test.q: Which set names the three attention networks in the Posner-Petersen model?
choices: Arousal, reward and motivational drive
Sensation, perception and short-term memory
Encoding, consolidation and retrieval
Alerting, orienting and executive control
test.explain: Posner and Petersen (1990) described alerting, orienting and executive control. The other sets describe perception, motivation and memory processes.

test.q: Which neurotransmitter is most closely tied to the alerting network?
choices: Acetylcholine
Norepinephrine
Dopamine
Serotonin
test.explain: Alerting depends on the locus coeruleus, which releases norepinephrine. Acetylcholine is linked mainly to orienting, and dopamine to executive control.

test.q: Which neurotransmitter, released from the basal forebrain, chiefly modulates the orienting network?
choices: Acetylcholine
Serotonin
Norepinephrine
Dopamine
test.explain: Basal forebrain acetylcholine modulates orienting. Norepinephrine is the tempting distractor, but it belongs to alerting.

test.q: Which brain region is most strongly engaged by Stroop and flanker conflict?
choices: Locus coeruleus
Primary somatosensory cortex
Cerebellar vermis
Anterior cingulate cortex
test.explain: The anterior cingulate cortex, together with lateral prefrontal cortex, is central to executive control of conflict. The locus coeruleus drives alerting instead.

test.q: What does covert orienting mean?
choices: Moving the eyes quickly toward a target
Ignoring a distracting item placed nearby
Becoming more alert after a warning tone
Shifting attention without moving the eyes
test.explain: Covert orienting shifts attention while gaze stays fixed. Moving the eyes is overt orienting.

test.q: In the Attention Network Test, how is the orienting score calculated?
choices: Incongruent RT minus congruent RT
Center-cue RT minus spatial-cue RT
Congruent RT minus neutral RT
No-cue RT minus double-cue RT
test.explain: A spatial cue tells you where the target will appear, while a center cue does not, so their difference isolates orienting. No-cue minus double-cue measures alerting.

test.q: In the Posner cueing task, when a cue points to the wrong location, responses are typically:
choices: Faster than after a valid cue
Slower than after a valid cue
Unaffected by the cue's direction
Faster than with no cue
test.explain: Invalid cues send attention to the wrong place, so it must be shifted, which slows responses. The difference from valid trials is the validity effect.

test.q: Damage to the right temporoparietal junction and inferior parietal lobule is classically linked to:
choices: Hemispatial neglect
Expressive aphasia
Loss of color vision
Face blindness
test.explain: Right TPJ and inferior parietal damage, part of the ventral attention network, causes neglect of the left side of space.

test.q: Naming the ink color of the word RED printed in blue mainly taxes which network?
choices: Alerting
Executive control
Ventral attention
Orienting
test.explain: The Stroop task creates conflict between reading the word and naming the color, and resolving that conflict is executive control.

test.q: Which tiny brainstem nucleus is the main source of norepinephrine for the alerting network?
test.explain: The locus coeruleus projects norepinephrine widely, including to right frontal and parietal cortex.

test.q: After an exogenous cue, the early speed advantage reverses after about 300 ms into a bias called inhibition of ___.
test.explain: Inhibition of return discourages re-inspecting a location that was just attended.

test.q: What is the full name of the task, published by Fan and colleagues in 2002, that measures alerting, orienting and conflict in one session?
test.explain: The ANT combines warning and spatial cues with a flanker task to score all three networks.

kidTest.q: Which helper wakes you up and says "Get ready!"?
choices: The control helper
The orienting helper
The alert helper
kidTest.explain: The alert helper gets you ready, like a referee's whistle.

kidTest.q: What does the orienting helper do?
choices: Points your spotlight at a place
Makes you feel sleepy and calm
Helps you remember old stories
kidTest.explain: Orienting moves your attention, like a spotlight, to where something is happening.

kidTest.q: In the arrow game, which arrow do you press the button for?
choices: The top arrow
The first arrow
The middle arrow
kidTest.explain: You answer for the way the middle arrow points and try to ignore the others.

kidTest.q: What does the control helper help you do?
choices: Hear very quiet sounds
See colors more brightly
Stop a wrong move
kidTest.explain: The control helper keeps you focused and stops you from doing the wrong thing.

kidTest.q: The three attention helpers work together as a t _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Each helper has its own brain parts, but they work together as a team.

advancedTest.q: A right TPJ stroke spares the dorsal FEF and IPS, yet the patient shows severe left neglect. Which explanation best fits the Corbetta model?
choices: The lesion removes norepinephrine supply to the whole cortex
Intact dorsal regions compensate, so the neglect is a sensory loss
Ventral damage unbalances the dorsal networks between hemispheres
TPJ damage blocks primary visual input arriving from the left eye
advancedTest.explain: Corbetta and colleagues proposed that ventral damage leaves dorsal regions structurally intact but functionally imbalanced across hemispheres, and this imbalance tracks severity and recovery. Neglect is an attentional disorder, not a primary sensory loss.

advancedTest.q: In the ANT-I, a warning tone speeds orienting but enlarges the flanker conflict effect. This finding most directly challenges:
choices: The idea that orienting can occur covertly
The use of reaction time to index conflict
The assumption that the networks act independently
The claim that alerting relies on norepinephrine release
advancedTest.explain: If alerting changes both orienting and conflict scores, the networks interact. The finding says nothing against the noradrenergic basis of alerting or covert orienting.

advancedTest.q: Under adaptive gain theory, a monkey with high baseline LC firing and weak task-locked bursts should show:
choices: Enhanced conflict resolution on incongruent trials
Drowsy disengagement with sluggish responses to cues
Focused, exploitative performance on the current task
Distractible, exploratory behavior with poor focus
advancedTest.explain: High tonic and weak phasic LC activity is the tonic mode, which favors exploration and distractibility. Focused exploitation belongs to the phasic mode, and drowsiness to low tonic firing.

advancedTest.q: A lab tests 40 adults and finds no link between a gene variant and ANT alerting scores, but a modest link with conflict scores. What is the best caution?
choices: The variant shapes conflict processing but not alertness
Larger samples would make the conflict link disappear
Alerting is better indexed by the flanker congruency difference
Alerting difference scores are noisy, so the null says little
advancedTest.explain: Alerting difference scores have poorer reliability than conflict scores, which caps observable correlations, so a small-sample null is weakly informative. Concluding that the variant does not affect alertness overinterprets that null.

lessons.title: How Attention Changes Neurons: Gain, Normalization and Synchrony

levels.kid:
Imagine your brain has a **flashlight**. When you pay attention to something, like a friend waving in a crowd, the flashlight shines on it.

Inside your brain, tiny cells called neurons notice what you see. When you pay attention, three things happen:

- The neurons looking at the waving friend get **louder**. They send more signals, like turning up the volume.
- The neurons looking at other things get **quieter**, so they don't get in the way.
- The busy neurons start to **sing together in rhythm**, like a choir, so their message travels better to the next part of the brain.

That is why paying attention helps you notice small things you might otherwise miss.
levels.hs:
Your eyes send far more information than your brain can fully process, so the brain has to choose. **Attention** is that choosing, and you can see it in single neurons.

Each visual neuron has a **receptive field**, the small patch of the world it watches. It reports what it sees by its **firing rate**, the number of electrical spikes per second. Attention changes these neurons in three main ways:

- **Gain**: attention works like a volume knob. A neuron watching the attended spot fires more, but it still prefers the same things. If it liked vertical lines before, it still likes vertical lines, just more strongly.
- **Normalization**: neurons divide down each other's activity. Each neuron's response is scaled by how active its neighbors are. Attention tips this competition so the attended object wins.
- **Synchrony**: attended neurons fire more in time with each other, often in the **gamma rhythm** (about 30 to 80 cycles per second). Spikes that arrive together have a bigger effect on the next brain area.

A famous example: in 1985, Jeffrey Moran and Robert Desimone recorded from area **V4** in monkeys. They placed two shapes inside one neuron's receptive field. When the monkey attended to one shape, the neuron responded almost as if the ignored shape were not there. Attention had filtered the world before it reached awareness.
levels.college:
Covert attention (attending without moving the eyes) changes how visual cortex neurons respond. Three families of effects have been measured.

**1. Gain changes.** McAdams and Maunsell (1999) measured orientation tuning curves in V4 with attention directed toward or away from the receptive field. Attention scaled the whole curve up, often by roughly 20-30%, without changing preferred orientation or tuning width. This is **multiplicative gain**. Effects grow along the hierarchy: modest in V1 (often under 10%), larger in V4, MT and parietal area LIP.

Gain is not just spatial. Treue and Martinez-Trujillo (1999) found in MT that attending to a motion direction raises responses of neurons preferring that direction across the visual field, even where nothing is attended. Neurons preferring the opposite direction are suppressed. This is **feature-similarity gain**.

**2. Competition and normalization.** Moran and Desimone (1985) showed that with two stimuli in one V4 receptive field, attention makes the response resemble the response to the attended stimulus alone. Desimone and Duncan's **biased competition** model explains this: stimuli compete for neural representation, and top-down signals bias the contest. **Divisive normalization**, in which each neuron's drive is divided by pooled activity of its neighbors, supplies the competitive machinery.

**3. Variability and synchrony.**
- Attention lowers trial-to-trial variability and reduces **noise correlations**, the shared fluctuations between neurons (Cohen and Maunsell 2009; Mitchell, Sundberg and Reynolds 2009).
- Fries and colleagues (2001) found that attention increased **gamma-band** (roughly 35-90 Hz) synchronization between V4 spikes and the local field potential, while reducing low-frequency synchronization.

In human fMRI, attention raises BOLD signals in visual areas including V1, and Kastner and colleagues (1999) showed activity rises at an attended location even before a stimulus appears, a **baseline shift**.
levels.phd:
The dominant unifying account is the **normalization model of attention** (Reynolds and Heeger 2009). A neuron's response is its stimulus drive multiplied by an attention field, divided by a suppressive pool plus a constant: R = (A·E) / (s∗(A·E) + σ), where s∗ denotes pooling over space and features. Because attention acts before normalization, its apparent effect depends on geometry:

- Small stimulus, broad attention field: attention scales the suppressive pool and the drive together, producing **contrast gain** (a leftward shift of the contrast-response function), as Martinez-Trujillo and Treue (2002) reported in MT.
- Large stimulus, narrow attention field: the drive rises more than the pool, producing **response gain** (higher saturating response), as Williford and Maunsell (2006) observed.

Herrmann, Carrasco, Heeger and colleagues (2010) confirmed these predictions psychophysically. Ni, Ray and Maunsell (2012) added that neurons with stronger tuned normalization show larger attentional modulation.

**Population coding.** Cohen and Maunsell (2009) recorded V4 populations with multielectrode arrays. Attention reduced pairwise noise correlations, and this reduction, not the rate increase, explained most of the gain in population sensitivity. The logic: independent noise can be averaged away across neurons, but correlated noise aligned with the signal cannot. Later modulator models (Rabinowitz and colleagues 2015) attribute much shared variability to a few fluctuating gain signals that attention dampens.

**Synchrony.** Fries's **communication through coherence** hypothesis (2005, revised 2015) proposes that a sender's gamma bursts reach a receiver during its excitable phase, so coherent pathways transmit while incoherent ones are gated out. Bosman and colleagues (2012) showed that V1 sites representing the attended stimulus selectively entrained V4 gamma.

**Controversy.** Ray and Maunsell (2015) noted that gamma frequency shifts with stimulus contrast and size, making it an unreliable fixed clock for routing, and gamma power can be weak for natural images. Critics propose gamma may be a byproduct of excitation-inhibition loops among parvalbumin interneurons rather than a causal routing signal. Whether coherence causes better transmission or simply reflects it remains unresolved.
levels.expert:
The modulations above need a source, and causal experiments point to frontoparietal and neuromodulatory inputs.

**Causal control.** Moore and Armstrong (2003) delivered microstimulation to the frontal eye field (FEF) below the threshold for evoking saccades and enhanced V4 responses at the matching location, mimicking attention. Gregoriou and colleagues (2009) found FEF-V4 gamma coherence rising with attention, with FEF leading in time. The pulvinar regulates alpha-band synchrony between visual areas (Saalmann and colleagues 2012).

**Neuromodulation.** Herrero and colleagues (2008) showed that blocking muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in macaque V1 reduced attentional modulation. Noudoost and Moore (2011) found that blocking D1 dopamine receptors in FEF enhanced V4 responses and selectivity. These results link cognitive pharmacology to circuit gain: cholinesterase inhibitors in Alzheimer's disease and catecholamine-raising stimulants in ADHD likely act partly on these prefrontal and cortical gain mechanisms.

**Clinical relevance.** Reduced gamma oscillations and impaired sensory gain control in schizophrenia are linked to parvalbumin interneuron dysfunction and NMDA receptor hypofunction, making gamma a candidate biomarker. Intracranial ECoG in epilepsy surgery patients shows attention-related high-gamma increases with millimetre precision, a resource for neurosurgery-adjacent research.

**Pitfalls.**
- **Microsaccades** are biased toward the attended location and themselves modulate V4 rates and gamma; Lowet and colleagues (2018) found attentional enhancement concentrated after microsaccades toward the target. Eye tracking is essential.
- Arousal, reward expectation and motor preparation can masquerade as attention unless controlled.
- Ruff and Cohen (2016) found attention increases correlations between V4 and MT even as it decreases them within V4, so correlation effects depend on which neurons share a task-relevant signal.

**Open questions.** Attention appears to fluctuate rhythmically rather than holding steady. Landau and Fries (2012) and Fiebelkorn, Pinsk and Kastner (2018) described roughly 4-8 Hz alternation between sampling and shifting states. Engel and colleagues (2016) found spontaneous on-off population states in V4 whose timing tracked attention. How theta rhythms, gain and gamma interlock, and whether interventions like closed-loop stimulation can restore them in disease, are active frontiers.

keyPoints: Attention multiplies neuronal responses (gain) without changing what they prefer
Feature-similarity gain boosts neurons tuned to an attended feature across the visual field
Divisive normalization supplies the competition that attention biases
The normalization model predicts contrast gain or response gain depending on stimulus and attention field size
Attention reduces noise correlations, which improves population coding
Attention increases gamma synchrony; communication through coherence remains debated

test.q: McAdams and Maunsell found that attention changes V4 orientation tuning curves mainly by:
choices: Scaling the whole curve up by a multiplicative factor
Shifting the preferred orientation toward the target
Making the curves much narrower and sharper
Reversing which orientation the neuron prefers
test.explain: Attention scaled tuning curves upward without changing preferred orientation or width, which is multiplicative gain.

test.q: Moran and Desimone placed two stimuli in one V4 receptive field. When the monkey attended to one, the neuron's response:
choices: Equaled the sum of responses to both stimuli
Dropped to zero for both of the stimuli
Matched its response to the ignored stimulus alone
Resembled its response to the attended stimulus alone
