test.explain: Attention made the neuron respond as if the ignored stimulus were absent, filtering out the unattended input.

test.q: In divisive normalization, a neuron's response is:
choices: Added to the activity of nearby neurons
Copied directly from the strongest neighbor
Divided by the pooled activity of nearby neurons
Set by the eye's position in the orbit
test.explain: Each neuron's drive is divided by the summed activity of a neighboring pool, creating competition that attention can bias.

test.q: Treue and Martinez-Trujillo found that attending to upward motion in MT:
choices: Silences MT neurons outside the attended location
Raises responses of neurons preferring downward motion
Boosts upward-preferring neurons at the attended spot alone
Boosts upward-preferring neurons across the visual field
test.explain: Feature-similarity gain applies across the visual field, even at unattended locations; neurons preferring the opposite direction are suppressed.

test.q: Fries and colleagues (2001) found that attention in V4 increased synchronization in which frequency range?
choices: The theta band near 6 Hz
The gamma band, roughly 35-90 Hz
The alpha band near 10 Hz
Slow delta waves below 4 Hz
test.explain: Attention increased gamma-band synchronization between spikes and the local field potential, while low-frequency synchronization decreased.

test.q: The communication through coherence hypothesis proposes that:
choices: Sender spikes arrive during the receiver's excitable phase
Signals travel faster along well-myelinated axons
Feedback from the eyes keeps cortical areas in step
Neurons fire faster in areas with higher blood flow
test.explain: If sender and receiver rhythms are coherent, input bursts land when the receiver is most excitable, so that pathway transmits effectively.

test.q: Cohen and Maunsell (2009) found that much of attention's benefit to V4 population coding came from:
choices: Larger receptive field sizes
Reduced noise correlations
Wider orientation tuning
Slower overall firing rates
test.explain: Attention reduced shared trial-to-trial fluctuations, and this explained most of the improvement in population sensitivity.

test.q: How does the size of spatial attention effects on firing rates usually compare across visual areas?
choices: They appear in V1 but vanish by area V4
They are largest in the retina and fade upstream
They are modest in V1 and larger in V4 and MT
They are similar in size across the visual areas
test.explain: Rate modulation is often under 10% in V1 and grows along the hierarchy into V4, MT and LIP.

test.q: The biased competition model of Desimone and Duncan states that:
choices: Competition happens in the retina before signals reach cortex
Stimuli compete for representation and top-down signals tip the contest
Neurons in each area process one stimulus at a time in sequence
The brightest stimulus in view wins regardless of the task
test.explain: Multiple stimuli compete for neural representation, and attention-related top-down signals bias the competition toward the relevant one.

test.q: Which brain rhythm, at roughly 30 to 80 cycles per second, becomes more synchronized among attended visual neurons?
test.explain: Gamma synchrony increases with attention and may help spikes arrive together at the next area.

test.q: Each neuron's drive is divided by the summed activity of its neighbors, a computation called divisive ___.
test.explain: Divisive normalization creates competition among neurons and is central to the Reynolds-Heeger model of attention.

test.q: In which visual area did Moran and Desimone first show attention filtering stimuli inside a receptive field? (Give the area name.)
test.explain: Their 1985 recordings in macaque V4 were among the first to show attention altering single-neuron responses.

kidTest.q: What happens to neurons looking at the thing you pay attention to?
choices: They stop working
They fall asleep
They get louder
kidTest.explain: Attention turns up their volume, so they send more signals.

kidTest.q: What happens to neurons looking at other things you are ignoring?
choices: They get quieter
They get louder too
They move to your ears
kidTest.explain: Quieter neighbors don't get in the way of the important signal.

kidTest.q: When busy neurons work together, what do they do, like a choir?
choices: Sing in rhythm
Take turns sleeping
Hide from each other
kidTest.explain: Firing together in rhythm helps their message travel to the next part of the brain.

kidTest.q: Why does paying attention help you?
choices: It helps you notice small things
It makes your eyes bigger
It makes the room brighter
kidTest.explain: Louder, rhythmic neurons help you notice details you might miss.

kidTest.q: Attention is like a f _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ that shines on what matters.
kidTest.explain: Like a flashlight, attention lights up one thing so you can see it better.

advancedTest.q: Per the Reynolds-Heeger model, attending broadly to a small, low-contrast stimulus inside a receptive field should mainly produce:
choices: A change in the neuron's preferred orientation toward the target
Response gain, raising the saturated response at high contrast
Contrast gain, shifting the contrast-response function leftward
Narrowing of the tuning curve with no change in firing rate
advancedTest.explain: When the attention field exceeds the stimulus, drive and suppressive pool are scaled together, producing contrast gain. Response gain is predicted for a large stimulus with a narrow attention field.

advancedTest.q: Why can a drop in noise correlations improve population coding more than a rise in firing rates?
choices: Lower correlations increase gamma frequency, speeding transmission overall
Correlated noise along the signal does not average out across neurons
Lower correlations make each neuron's receptive field noticeably larger
Higher firing rates tend to lower a neuron's preferred orientation
advancedTest.explain: Independent noise averages out across a population, but shared noise aligned with the signal does not, so reducing it raises population sensitivity.

advancedTest.q: Ray and Maunsell's critique of communication through coherence centers on the finding that:
choices: Gamma oscillations arise in the retina rather than in visual cortex
Gamma coherence between V1 and V4 appears without any visual input
Gamma frequency shifts with stimulus contrast, weakening its role as a clock
Gamma power is unaffected when attention is directed to a stimulus
advancedTest.explain: If gamma frequency varies with stimulus features, separate populations may not share a stable rhythm, undermining a fixed-frequency routing mechanism.

advancedTest.q: A monkey attends to upward motion in the left visual field. Under feature-similarity gain, an MT neuron with a right-field receptive field that prefers downward motion should show:
choices: Increased firing if a downward stimulus appears on the left
No change, since its receptive field is outside the attended area
Increased firing, since attention boosts MT activity broadly
Decreased firing, as it prefers the opposite direction
advancedTest.explain: Feature-similarity gain operates across the visual field and scales responses by similarity to the attended feature; neurons preferring the opposite direction are suppressed.
